method: The monostatic radar range equation sets the echo power at the receiver equal to the minimum detectable signal and solves for range: R_max = [P_t G^2 lambda^2 sigma / ((4 pi)^3 S_min L)]^(1/4), where P_t is peak transmit power in watts, G is the antenna gain as a linear power ratio (10^(dBi/10), entered once because the same antenna transmits and receives), lambda = c / f with c = 299,792,458 m/s, sigma is the target radar cross section in square metres, S_min is the receiver sensitivity in watts (entered in dBm and converted with 10^((dBm - 30)/10)), and L is the total system loss as a linear factor (10^(dB/10)). The echo at any range R is P_t G^2 lambda^2 sigma / ((4 pi)^3 R^4 L), so it falls by 6 dB per doubling of range twice over, a 1/R^4 law; the reported margin is that echo in dBm minus the entered sensitivity, and the round-trip time is 2R / c. Because range enters the equation to the fourth power, doubling the detection range needs sixteen times the power, sixteen times the radar cross section, four times the antenna gain, or 12 dB less loss. Inputs are bounded to keep the arithmetic in ordinary double precision: peak power 0.0001 to 1,000,000 W, gain 0 to 80 dBi, frequency 0.001 to 300 GHz, radar cross section 0.0001 to 1,000,000 m^2, system losses 0 to 100 dB, sensitivity -200 to 0 dBm and evaluation range 0.1 to 10,000,000 m. The model assumes free-space two-way propagation, a non-fluctuating point target of constant radar cross section, matched polarisation, and a single lumped loss term; it does not model atmospheric or rain absorption, multipath or ground reflection, clutter, the radar horizon, pulse integration, Swerling target fluctuation, or the probability of detection and false alarm behind the sensitivity figure, and a real radar's detection range also depends on the signal processing and the environment. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Skolnik, Introduction to Radar Systems: the monostatic radar range equation relates received echo power to peak transmit power, antenna gain squared, wavelength squared, radar cross section and the inverse fourth power of range, with the maximum range found where the echo equals the minimum detectable signal.

The (4 pi)^3 factor comes from the two-way spherical spreading: power density falls as 1/(4 pi R^2) on the way out and the same again on the return, after the target re-radiates the intercepted power in proportion to its radar cross section.
Antenna gain in dBi is a logarithmic power ratio, G = 10^(dBi/10); a 30 dBi antenna has a linear gain of 1000, and using the dBi number directly in the equation is a common error.
A power in dBm converts to watts as P = 10^((dBm - 30)/10), so -100 dBm is 10^-13 W; system loss in dB converts to a linear factor as L = 10^(dB/10).

Published worked examples used to check the arithmetic: a 1 MW S-band radar with 40 dBi gain, 1 m^2 target, 6 dB loss and -98 dBm sensitivity gives about 168 km, and a 12 kW X-band marine radar with 31 dBi gain, 10 m^2 target, 8 dB loss and -92 dBm sensitivity gives about 12.5 km.
